activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Avery sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house today. "Is it now?" she asked. "Yes, we are driving now," said Mama.

Yesterday, Avery had dropped her bunny at Grandma's house. She missed bunny. Tomorrow was bunny's tea party. But today was the day to get bunny back.

Avery looked out the window. The sun was in her eye. It made a warm spot on her sleeve. Then the car turned. A big truck went by. The warm spot went away. Where did it go? "The truck made shade," said Mama. The truck was gone now, and the sun came back. The warm spot was back too.

Avery wiggled her ear. She heard the turn signal. Click, click. The car turned left. That meant Grandma's street. Later they would have cookies. But first, the car stopped. Grandma stood at the door. She held something soft and thin, with long ears. "Bunny missed you," said Grandma. Avery held out both arms. "Now we can go home together," she said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Nova went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so the slide was wet. Nova touched the slide. Her hand got drippy. "I want to slide now," she said.

Dad opened his bag. He pulled out a small towel. He wiped the slide, top to bottom. The wet went away. The slide was dry now. Nova climbed up. She slid down fast. "Again," she said. She slid down three more times.

Later, Nova saw a big puddle by the swings. The sun was warm on her back. They waited and waited. Nova watched the puddle get smaller and smaller. Then the puddle was gone. Dad kissed her head. "We will come back tomorrow," he said. "Maybe the ducks will be in the pond." Nova laughed. "Ducks are funny," she said. She ran to the gate.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Elias sits in a big chair at the doctor's office. Dad holds his hand. The nurse has a small bandage and a tiny white stick.

"Will it hurt?" asks Elias.

"Just a quick pinch," says Dad.

The nurse taps Elias's arm. "Look at your hand," she says. Elias opens his fingers, one by one. While he looks down, the nurse gives the shot. Elias feels the pinch. Then the pinch goes away.

"It is done!" says Elias. He got a shiny red bandage. The nurse gives him a sticker of a happy dog. Elias smiles.

"What made the pinch stop hurting?" Elias asks Dad.

"Playing helps it stop," says Dad.

So Elias squeezes his teddy bear tight. The pinch feels smaller. Then Dad lets him jump to the door. The pinch feels smaller still.

Afterward they go to the ice cream shop. Elias picks pink ice cream. He licks it. "Dad! The pinch is all gone!" he says.

Elias lifts his arm up high. He waves the red bandage at the ice cream man.

"Vanilla or strawberry?" the man asks.

"Strawberry, please," says Elias.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Raphael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make a card for his dad. Grandma gave him red paper and glue.

Raphael spread the glue on the paper. He stuck on a cotton ball. It looked like a fluffy cloud. He stuck on more and more. Soon the card was full.

Then Raphael pushed a cotton ball with his finger. Squishy! The glue came up through the cotton. It felt cold and sticky on his skin. He pushed another one. Squish! More glue came out.

"Look, Grandma!" he said. "The glue comes up when I push!"

"That happens with wet glue," said Grandma. "Let's add one more cloud."

They pushed one more cotton ball together. Then they set the card by the window. Raphael watched it all afternoon. The glue dried and the cotton balls stopped being sticky.

"Is it ready now?" he asked.

"It is ready," said Grandma.

Raphael held the card up high. "Dad will love his fluffy clouds!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Anthony sat with Mom and Dad at a big table. A big screen glowed on the wall. It showed a football game. Everyone was excited. Uncle Ben waved his hands. Aunt Mia clapped.

Anthony wanted to see the game too. But the tall man in front of him sat right in the way. Anthony stood on his toes. He still could not see. "I can't see!" he said.

Then Anthony had a smart idea. He pulled his chair to the side, near Aunt Mia. Now the tall man was not in the way. Anthony could see the whole screen. The players ran. The crowd on the screen made a big noise.

The whole restaurant made a big noise too. Everyone jumped up. "They did it!" Dad shouted. Anthony clapped and clapped. Uncle Ben sent a fry flying across the table. Anthony laughed and caught it in his cup. Aunt Mia hugged him tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
It was sharing day at school. Willow had a big red bag. She wanted to show her toy bunny to the class. But when she opened the bag, the bunny was not there. Only an apple was inside.

"Oh no," said Willow. "My bunny is gone."

Her teacher, Miss Pam, came to help. "Let's look together," she said. They looked in the cubby. They looked under the rug. Then Willow had an idea. The apple was a food, not a toy. Somebody might have her bag by mistake.

Tommy sat at the next table. His bag was red too, the same color. He opened it and pulled out a soft gray bunny.

"That's my bunny!" said Willow.

"And this apple is mine," said Tommy. "My mom packed it today."

They traded bags and laughed. Willow learned that looking closely was a good tool for finding lost things. She hugged her bunny tight.

"Now we both have the right things," said Willow. Tommy took a big bite of his apple.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Sofia stood by the kitchen table. Mom had made warm toast, but Mom was busy with the baby. Sofia wanted to butter her own toast today.

She picked up the butter knife. Mom had put soft butter in a little dish. Sofia dipped the knife in. She pressed hard on the toast. The bread tore, and a big lump of butter sat in one spot. "Hmm," said Sofia. She looked at the lump. Would the toast rip again?

She tried again, easy this time. She touched the butter lightly. Then she slid the knife across, slow and gentle. The butter went on thin. It spread from edge to edge. The whole slice turned shiny and yellow. "It pays to go slow," Mom said with a smile, peeking over.

Next came the milk. Sofia held the small cup with one hand. She held the little pitcher with the other. She poured fast, and milk splashed onto the table. She stopped. She wiped it up with a towel. She tried once more, tipping the pitcher just a little. The milk ran in a thin white line. It went all the way to the top. Not one drop spilled.

Sofia took a bite of her toast. The butter tasted real and sweet. "I did it myself," she said, and she raised her cup like a tiny queen.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Anthony looked out the window. Snow was falling on the grass. Snow was falling on the car. School was closed today!

"Snow day!" Anthony shouted. He jumped up and down. "Can we play outside, Mom?"

"Yes," said Mom. "But your boots are wet from yesterday."

Anthony frowned. He wanted his boots now. He looked at his boots by the door. They were dark with water. Mom put them near the warm heater. "We will wait a little," she said.

Anthony waited. He counted the snowflakes on the window. One, two, three. He drew a rainbow with his crayons. One, two, three colors. Then he touched his boot. It was still wet. He touched it again later. It was warm and dry!

"The heater made my boots dry!" said Anthony. "Now can we go outside?"

Mom laughed. "Yes, little snow bunny. Boots on!"

Anthony pulled on his warm, dry boots. He ran out the door. The snow went crunch, crunch under his feet. He made one big snowball. He made one small snowball. He put the small one on top. "Hello, Mr. Snowman," said Anthony. "You need a carrot nose."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Myles went to Dad's office. He saw a tablet on the desk. "Can I draw?" he asked. "You can," said Dad. "First you push the little button."

Myles pushed the button. The screen lit up. He pushed it again and the screen went dark. He laughed. He pushed once more and the light came back. "Like magic," he said. Dad showed him the drawing app. Myles tapped it. A white page opened. He drew a big sun and a red car on a busy street. He drew his dad smiling next to him.

Soon the tablet looked tired, just like Myles. "Time to put it away," said Dad. Myles pushed the button and the screen went dark. He folded the cover over it, slow and careful. He set it on the desk. Then he took Dad's hand and said, "Now can we draw on paper too?"

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Liam turned three today. His party was at the big park. Grandma brought a cake with candles on top.

Dad lit the candles with a match. "Watch the little flames," said Dad. Liam puffed air from his mouth at them. One flame went out. He puffed again. Another flame went out. Liam laughed. He puffed and puffed until every flame was gone.

"Make a wish!" said Mom. Liam closed his eyes. Then he clapped his hands. The candles stayed dark. "No more flames," he said. "That is true," said Grandma. "You blew them all out, big boy."

After cake, Liam and his cousin Ben walked to the pond. They held paper cups of duck food. Liam threw some food in the water. A duck swam over fast. He threw more food. More ducks came. "The ducks think it is their birthday too," said Ben. Liam threw the last bit. The biggest duck gobbled it up.

"Happy birthday, ducks," said Liam.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Matteo had a library book about trucks. He loved it so much. He wanted to keep it forever.

Mama sat with him on the big sofa. She opened the front cover first. "We start here," she said. She pointed at the little black marks on the page. Her finger slid under them. "Truck," she read. The picture popped up. A big red truck! The marks told Mama what to say. Matteo put his own finger under the marks. "Truck!" he said. Every page had more marks. More words. He turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back.

Then Mama said, "We have a problem. The book belongs to the library. Other kids want to read it too. We take it back soon." Matteo held the book tight to his chest. "My book," he said. His eyes got hot and watery.

Mama hugged him close. "We can borrow it again," she said. "And we can pick fresh books too." So they went back to the library. Matteo gave the truck book to the librarian. She smiled and put a stamp on a card. Then Matteo found a new book about diggers. He opened the front cover. He put his finger under the marks.

"Digger!" said Matteo.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Rose sat in a big seat at the stadium. The game was down on the green field. But a tall man sat right in front of her. She could not see the players at all.

"Daddy, I can't see," said Rose. Dad planted his feet, held her hands, and lifted her up. Now Rose could see everything. She saw the players run. She saw the red and yellow hats all around.

Then Rose spotted a man with a camera. The camera was looking at the crowd. Rose began to wave her arms, big and slow. The camera man pointed at her. Rose looked up at the giant screen. There she was, waving, right next to Dad's head. She waved even faster. The whole crowd made a noise like a storm, loud and happy. Mom laughed and waved too.

"Look at us!" said Rose. She waved until her arm was tired.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Max got on the big yellow bus. He sat by the window. He held his little red backpack tight.

The bus door closed with a whoosh. Then the bus began to roll. Max looked out. The trees went by. The houses went by. When the bus stopped, the door opened. When the bus went, the door shut again. Max tapped the window with his finger. "Stop means open," he said. "Go means shut."

A girl sat down next to him. Her name was Lily. "Want to see?" Max asked. The bus stopped, and the door opened. Lily clapped her hands. "You teach me the bus!" she said.

At school, the driver smiled. "Have a sweet first day," she said. Max waved. Then he took Lily's hand and walked to his classroom door.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Sienna went to the store with Dad. She wanted apples for snack time. Dad said, "Let's pick ten apples."

Sienna held the bag. She put one apple in. Then she put two more. Dad said, "One, two, three."

Sienna counted too. "Four, five, six." The apples rolled in the bag. She dropped one. It rolled under the shelf. Dad got down low. He reached slowly. He waited. Then his hand came out with the apple.

"Seven," said Sienna. She put in one more. "Eight." Dad handed her one. "Nine."

"One more," said Dad. Sienna looked in the bin. She picked a big red apple. She held it with both hands. She set it in softly. "Ten!"

At home, Dad washed the apples. Sienna watched the water dance down the sides. Dad gave her one apple, cut in slices. The messy juice ran down her chin. She counted her slices. "One, two, three, four." Then she ate every one.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Logan ran to the big window. He wanted to play outside. "Look, Mommy, it is sunny!" he said. The sun made a warm spot on the floor. Logan put his hand in the sun spot. It felt warm, like toast.

He put on his sun hat. He found his little shoes. Then the sky turned gray. Tap, tap, tap. Rain hit the window. "Oh no," said Logan. "Now it is rainy!" Mommy gave him his red rain boots. She gave him his rain coat with the hood. Logan jumped in a puddle. Splash! His boots kept his socks dry.

A big wind came. It was windy! The wind blew his hood off his head. The wind blew the leaves round and round. Logan held his hat with both hands. "My hat almost flew away!" he laughed.

Then white flakes fell down. "Snowy!" Logan shouted. He caught one on his glove. The snowflake melted into a tiny wet dot. Soon Logan was cold and sleepy, like a tired puppy with a tired bone. Mommy brought him in. She wrapped him in a soft blanket. "Warm cocoa?" she asked. Logan nodded and held his cup with both hands.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Gabriel ran to the playground. The sun was hot. His slide was hot too. He touched it. "Ouch!" He pulled his hand back fast.

He wanted to slide, but the slide was too hot. What could he do? He looked around. The big kids were slow and careful on the hot slide. The small kids sat in the shade. Gabriel sat in the shade too. He drank cold water from his bottle. It was quiet under the tree.

Then the clouds came. The sun went away. Gabriel touched the slide again. Now it was cold! He climbed up fast. He slid down. "Whee!" He splashed in a little puddle at the bottom. His mom gave him a towel for his wet shoes. "Again!" said Gabriel.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Juliette was on the swim team. The team met at the big pool every week. Coach Ana gave each kid a kickboard.

Juliette held the board tight. She kicked her legs fast. Kick, kick, kick. The water made splashes. And Juliette moved! She moved all the way to the rope.

But then her legs got tired. She stopped kicking. The splashes stopped too. And Juliette stopped moving. She stayed right there, floating like a little boat.

"Look at you," said Coach Ana. "You went so far." Juliette frowned. "I stopped," she said. "I want to go to the rope again."

Coach Ana smiled. "Try small kicks. Little ones." Juliette kicked small and slow. Kick, kick, kick. The splashes came back. Juliette moved again, slow and steady, all the way to the rope. The tall girl on the team clapped for her.

After swim time, Juliette sat with her dad by the pool. They shared a snack. "Swim team makes me hungry," she said. Dad laughed. "Then it's a good thing it's dinner time soon."

Juliette looked at the water. "Kick, kick, kick," she said softly, and her feet wiggled under the towel.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Brooklyn stood at the bus stop with Grandma. The wind blew. Her coat was in her arms, not on her.

"I want to do it myself," said Brooklyn. She pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The coat hung crooked. One sleeve was empty.

"Try again," said Grandma. "We can wait for the bus."

Brooklyn counted her arms. "One arm. Two arms." She pulled the coat on. Now it was straight. She felt the furry collar on her chin. It was soft.

Next came the zipper. She held the bottom. She pushed the little part in. Click. She pulled it up. Up, up, up. The zipper made a loud zzzip sound.

"Now I am warm," said Brooklyn. The wind blew again. This time the wind did not get in.

Grandma smiled. "The bus is coming," she said.

Brooklyn zipped her coat all the way to the top. "Zzzip!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Audrey had a cough. She wanted it to go away. Mom said, "We will call the pharmacy." Mom picked up the phone. The man there said he had medicine for coughs.

Mom took Audrey to the pharmacy. It was bright inside. Audrey saw boxes and bottles on the shelves. The man gave Mom a small bottle. "Take this at home," he said. Audrey held Mom's hand tight. The floor was slippery, so she walked slowly.

At home, Mom poured a spoon of medicine. It tasted like cherry. Audrey swallowed it. She rested on the couch. She coughed less. Then she coughed even less. "My cough is going away," Audrey said. Mom pulled the blanket up. "Look at that," said Mom. Audrey smiled and hugged her teddy bear.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Mia was four years old today. The sky was cloudy, but the party was still on. Her friends came to the big park. There were balloons and hats for everyone.

Dad put the cake on the table. He lit the four little candles. Mia wanted to blow them out. But her friend Sam was sad. His balloon had flown away. Mia gave him one of her own. Sam smiled big.

Then everyone sang the birthday song. Mia took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four candles went out. Up went little curls of smoke. Mia laughed. "Look! The smoke goes up when the candles go out!" she said. Mom cut the cake with the big knife. Mia helped pass out plates. After cake, Grandpa was sleepy. He took his nap under a tree. Dad clicked the cooler closed to lock in the ice. Mia waved her smoke curl goodbye.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Dylan sat in the waiting room. He wanted to eat his crackers. But his hands felt sticky.

The nurse came by with a big smile. "Time to wash hands first," she said. Dylan ran to the little sink. He put his hands under the water. He pumped the soap. Bubbles came out!

"Look at that!" said Dylan. He rubbed his palms together. The bubbles grew and grew. He rubbed the backs of his hands. More bubbles! He rubbed between his fingers. The sticky spots went away.

"How long do I rub?" Dylan asked. "We sing the happy song," said the nurse. They sang it together. "Happy birthday to you!" When the song was done, the bubbles rinsed off. The water carried them down the drain.

Dylan held up his hands. They were clean and shiny. He smelled them. "Mmm, like flowers!" he said. He looked at his hands all over. The sticky was gone. The world looked ready for crackers now.

Dylan ran back to his chair. He picked up a cracker with his clean fingers. Crunch! It tasted so good. "My hands are clean, so my cracker stays clean," said Dylan. The nurse gave him a thumbs up. Dylan grinned and took another big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Asher went to the store with Mama. It was a rainy day. The floor was wet near the door.

Asher wanted a red apple. He looked in the big bin. He saw green apples too. He reached for a red one.

"Can I hold it?" he asked.

"Yes," said Mama. "Hold it gently."

The red apple felt smooth and cold. Asher put it in the cart. Then he saw bananas. They were yellow. "I want one," he said. Mama put three yellow bananas in the cart.

Next they passed the milk. The carton was blue like the sky. Asher tapped it. "Blue!" he said. A man nearby smiled.

At the wall, Asher saw green balloons. He touched one. It slid down the string and bounced back up. Asher laughed and did it again.

"Time to pay," said Mama. Asher helped put the red apple on the counter. He heard the beep, beep of the register.

They walked out into the rain. Asher held Mama's hand tight. He carried the bag with the yellow bananas.

"My apple is in here," he said.

"Yes," said Mama. "We will wash it and eat it at home."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Romy wanted to make tea for her teddy bear. But the tea set had a big pot and one small cup. The big pot was too big for one small bear.

First she needed real tea. Dad filled the kettle. The kettle got hot, so Dad poured the tea. "Careful, it's hot," said Dad. Romy watched from her step stool. She blew on the cup. She blew slow puffs. Then she touched the side. "Cold now," she said. The tea had gone from hot to cold.

Romy poured the small cup for teddy. Then she ran fast around the playroom with him. The tea spilled. "Too fast," said Romy. So she walked slow, holding the cup with two hands. Not one drop spilled.

Just then teddy slipped. His tea went all over the floor. Romy felt mad for a second. Then she saw something. The spill made a big wet spot on the rug. She dropped one small drop of tea next to it. The small drop made a small spot.

"Dad! Big spills make big spots," said Romy. "Small drops make small ones." Dad smiled and brought a towel. Romy wiped up the big spot first. Then she wiped the small one. "Teach me the slow walk again," said teddy's voice, and Dad laughed. Romy held her bear close and gave him one more small drop.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Naomi stood in the reading corner. She was four years old today. Her mama knelt down beside her. "You can try for your very own library card," Mama said.

The librarian smiled. She gave Naomi a small card. It was red and white. It said Naomi on it. Naomi held it with both hands.

Then Naomi found a book. It had a bear on the cover. The bear was making a big circle in the snow. "I want this one," said Naomi. "Forever and ever."

The librarian shook her head softly. "You can take it home. But you must bring it back. Then other kids can read it too. I will mark the day it is due."

Naomi frowned. She did not want to let the bear book go. But then a boy came in. He was looking for a bear book. He looked sad.

Naomi thought and thought. She could read it lots of times at home. Then she could bring it back. The boy could have a turn.

"Okay," she said. "I will bring it back." The librarian stamped the card. Naomi put the book in her bag. She hugged the bag all the way home.

At bedtime, they read about the bear and his circle in the snow. "Again," said Naomi. "Read it again."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Layla wants to help make a cake for Grandma. It is a gift for Grandma's visit.

Mama says, "First we wash our hands." Layla washes her hands. Her wet hands feel cold. She touches the soft flour. It is white and light. Then she touches the sugar bowl. The sugar feels like little sand.

Mama cracks the eggs. Layla listens. Tap, tap. The bowl sounds like that. Then Mama turns on the mixer. It is loud. Layla covers her ears. She waits until it is quiet again.

The cake goes in the oven. Mama puts it in, not Layla. The oven is hot. Soon Layla smells something sweet. "I can smell it with my nose!" she says. They wait and wait. Layla watches the oven door.

At last the cake is out. It is cool now. Mama cuts a little piece. Layla puts it in her mouth. It tastes sweet and yummy. "Grandma will love it," says Layla. She jumps up and down. The heavy cake sits safe on the table, waiting for Grandma.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Paisley sat in her car seat. Today was the day for Grandma's house. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Later, after the sun goes past that big tree."

Paisley looked out the window. Yesterday she had seen a wild goose by the pond. The goose was gone today. "Where did it go?" she asked. "Maybe it will come back tomorrow," said Mom. Paisley watched and watched, but no goose came.

"I want to see Grandma now," said Paisley. "We get there later," said Mom. "First we drive. Then we stop. Then we are there." Paisley tapped her shoes. One, two, three. She saw the sun move past the tree. She saw the road bend. Then the car stopped, and Grandma opened the door.

Paisley ran to her. Grandma held out her hand. In it was one small white egg. "The hen laid this today," said Grandma. "Yesterday there was no egg. Tomorrow there may be one more." Paisley held the egg very carefully. "Can we look for another one tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma smiled and took her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Audrey was in the playroom with her friend Ben. There was one big red truck. They both wanted it.

Audrey grabbed the truck. Ben grabbed it too. The truck tipped over. Blocks went everywhere. Some water from a small cup did spill on the rug.

Mama came in. She sat down on the soft rug. "Let's try the timer," she said. Mama turned the timer. It went tick, tick, tick.

Audrey pushed the truck. "Vroom," she said. She made a slow ramp with one block. Then the timer rang. Now it was Ben's turn. Audrey gave him the truck. Ben pushed it fast. Then the timer rang again. Back to Audrey.

Ben said, "I like the ramp. What is its name?" Audrey said, "His name is Truckey." Ben laughed. They counted the blocks together. One, two, three, four.

Audrey found one more cookie in her pocket. She broke it in half. She gave the big half to Ben. "You take this one," she said. Ben said, "Thank you, Audrey." The timer ticked on the shelf. They played until snack time. "Your turn, Ben," said Audrey.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Charlie was at soccer practice. The coach had one big red ball. Charlie wanted it first.

Milo held the ball. Charlie ran up and grabbed it. The ball popped out of both hands. It rolled under the bench. Milo sat down and did not smile.

The coach got the ball out. She gave it back to Milo. "Your turn first, Milo," she said. Charlie put his hands behind his back. He waited. He counted his shoes. One, two. Still he waited.

Then Milo kicked the ball. It rolled right to Charlie. "Now you," said Milo. Charlie laughed. The ball came to him when he waited! He kicked it back. Milo kicked it again. The ball went back and forth, back and forth.

"Nice waiting, Charlie," said the coach. She put a gold star sticker on his shirt. Milo gave him a friendly pat on the back. At juice time, Charlie let Milo go first in the line. Milo sent him a big grin.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a little scratchy sound, like a tiny cat at the door. She wanted bread, and she wanted it now.

"Mama, is the bread done?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. "It is baking now. We will eat it later."

Iris sighed. Waiting made her feel a little mad. She watched the oven door. Then she smelled it. Warm bread, bread, bread.

"Yesterday we had soup," said Mama. "Today we have bread. Tomorrow we will have berries."

Iris counted on her plate. "Yesterday, today, tomorrow." One, two, three.

Then the oven beeped. Mama opened the door. The bread came out, big and warm.

"Is it now?" asked Iris.

"It is now," said Mama.

Iris took a big, soft bite.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Milo wanted his red truck. It rolled under the big bed. He got down on his knees. He could see the truck way in the back. His arm was too short.

Milo went to find Dad. "Dad, can you help me, please?" he asked. Dad smiled. He got down on the floor too. Dad reached far under the bed. Out came the shiny red truck.

"Thank you!" said Milo. He gave Dad a hug.

Then Milo ran fast with his truck. He bumped into the cat's water bowl. Water went all over the floor. "Sorry, cat," said Milo. The cat licked one wet paw.

Dad brought a towel. Milo helped wipe the floor. It took a long time. They wiped and wiped. At last the floor was dry and shiny.

Milo set the bowl back in its spot. He put his truck beside it, nice and safe. "Good spot," said Dad. The cat curled up on the bed for a nap.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
James sat at the big art table. He had a pot of red paint and a pot of blue paint. His teacher had asked everyone to paint a frog. James wanted to paint a green frog. But he looked and looked. There was no green paint.

He looked at his friend Mia. She had yellow paint. She made a big yellow sun. James wanted green, not yellow. He sighed and tapped his brush.

Then he dipped his brush in the red pot. He made a red frog on his paper. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue pot. He painted blue over the red frog. He waited for it to dry. The frog turned green!

"Look, look!" said James. "My frog is green now!" Mia came to see. She dipped her brush in yellow. Then she dipped it in blue. She made a blue-yellow pond for the frog. The pond turned green too.

"Green pond for a green frog," said Mia.

James smiled. Green was his new favorite color. He added one more dot of red. It turned into a little green bug.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Lily stood on a little stool in the big restaurant kitchen. She wanted to make breakfast all by herself.

"Can I butter the toast?" she asked.

"Yes," said Cook. He cut warm bread for her. Lily held the butter knife. She pressed too hard. The toast tore into holes.

"That is not good," said Lily.

"Try little strokes," said Cook. "Go slow and be gentle." Lily made soft little strokes. The butter sat on top, shiny and smooth.

"Now the milk," said Cook. He set the jug high on the counter and tipped it for her. Milk splashed over the cup edge. Lily gasped. She watched the cup. She poured slowly. The milk went up, up. It stopped right at the rim.

"No spill," said Lily.

Cook hung a star next to her name on the kitchen map. Lily spread butter on one more slice, just for Dad.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Ella went to the pet store with Dad. A bell went ring as the door opened. Ella looked at the cages. She looked at the tanks. Then she saw a little orange fish. "That one," said Ella. Dad said, "Okay. That fish comes home with us."

The shop lady put the fish in a bag. The bag was full of water. Ella held one side, and Dad held the other. "The bag is heavy," said Ella. "Hold it strong," said Dad. They walked home slow. The fish swam in small circles.

At home, Dad poured the fish into its bowl. Ella wanted to feed it. She shook the food jar, and lots of flakes fell in. The flakes covered the top of the water. Dad took them out with a little net. "Just two flakes," said Dad. Ella put in two flakes. The fish came up and ate one. Ella put in two more, and the fish ate those too. "You like your food," said Ella. The fish blew a tiny bubble.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Ayla went to the band room with her class. She wanted to play the big drum. The teacher, Mr. Bell, said, "You can try, Ayla." Ayla tapped the drum with her little hand. It made a tiny sound. "Why is it so quiet?" she asked. "Try the drumstick," said Mr. Bell. Ayla picked up the drumstick. She tapped once, soft. Tum. She tapped again, hard. BOOM! The big sound filled the room. "I did that!" said Ayla. She tapped soft, then hard. Tum, BOOM. Tum, BOOM. The band children looked up and smiled.

At home, Ayla told Mama all about it. "We can shop for a little drum for you," said Mama. Mama pulled the zipper on Ayla's coat, straight up to her chin. "Can I play it every day?" asked Ayla. "Yes," said Mama. Ayla smiled and patted her knees. Tum, BOOM. Tum, BOOM.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her cup was empty. "More milk, please," she said. Dad poured the milk. "Thank you," said Sienna. Dad smiled big.

Then Sienna reached for the bread. It was far away. She stretched. She stretched more. The basket began to tip. CRASH. The bread rolled under the table. "Sorry," Sienna said quietly. "That's okay," said Mom. "Ask for help next time."

Sienna slid down from her chair. She counted the bread rolls under the table. One, two, three. She reached for them. One, two, three back in the basket. Mom held the basket while Sienna put them in.

Now Sienna wanted the butter. She remembered the bread basket. She did not stretch. "Mom, can you help me, please?" she asked. Mom passed the butter. "Thank you," said Sienna. She buttered her bread all by herself. "Yummy," she said, and took a big bite. Dad raised his milk cup. "To Sienna," he said. "To Sienna," said Mom. Sienna raised her cup too. "To me," she said.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Camille sat down at the dinner table. There was one big bowl of peas. Daddy put some peas on her plate. Then he put some on Ben's plate. Camille looked at the two plates. They had the same amount. "How does he know?" she wondered.

Camille wanted the yellow cup. But Ben had the yellow cup. Ben saw her face. He drank a little sip. Then he slid the cup across the table. "Your turn," he said. Camille smiled. She took a sip. Then she slid it back. Back and forth the cup went, like a little boat.

A tiny bug walked on the window. Camille watched it. The bug went up. Then the bug went down. "Even the bug takes turns going up and down," she thought. Daddy used a knife to cut the bread. He cut one piece for Camille. He cut one piece for Ben. Same size again.

Then Daddy brought out the smelly cheese. Camille held her nose. "Pee-yew!" she said. Daddy laughed and cut the cheese into small bits. He put one bit on her plate. Camille touched it with one finger. She sniffed it close. "Still smelly," she said, "but I will try a tiny bite."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Jaxson wanted warm cocoa. His tummy was hungry for it. He stood next to Grandma in the kitchen. "Stay right here," said Grandma. "I will stay close," said Jaxson.

Grandma turned on the stove. The pot began to hum. Then steam rose up from the pot. The steam went high, like a little cloud. "The steam is hot," said Grandma. "Watch, do not touch." Jaxson watched the steam dance. He took one step back.

Then the pot was taken off the stove. Grandma poured the cocoa into a cup. Jaxson touched the cup with just one finger. The cup was warm, not too hot. "You waited so well," said Grandma. Jaxson sat by her feet and drank slowly. The lazy cat came over and sniffed his cup. "Not for you," said Jaxson. He smiled and took another little sip.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Bennett stood by his bedroom window. Yesterday it rained. He could not go on the swing. "Where is the sun now?" he asked. Mama smiled. "The sun is here now," she said. "Look. Now the sky is blue." Bennett saw the round yellow sun. It made a warm spot on his bed.

Today the sun was out. "Can we swing today?" Bennett asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We will swing after lunch. First we eat, then later we swing." Bennett clapped his hands. "Later we swing," he said. "Later we swing!" He put his bear on the bed. The sun spot moved. It moved from the pillow to the floor. Bennett watched it go. The sun was making the spot move, little by little.

After lunch, Mama called him. "It is later now," she said. Bennett ran outside. He sat on the swing. Mama pushed him, up and up. Bennett laughed. "The sun is up too," he said. "Tomorrow can we swing again?" "Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow is a new day, just like today." Bennett swung high and touched his toes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. She was very hungry. Mom had made a surprise.

"What is it?" Rosalie asked.

"Look in the pot," said Mom.

Rosalie peeked in. She saw carrots and peas and noodles. "Foods!" she shouted. "So many foods!"

Then she saw something small in her cup. It was her toy duck. It had fallen in the water.

"Oh no," said Rosalie. "My duck is thirsty too!"

She pulled the duck out. It was all wet. She gave it a little pat with her napkin.

The duck sat on the table by her plate. Rosalie held it up. "Do you like carrots?" she made the duck speak in a small voice. "Quack, quack, yes!"

Mom laughed. "Your duck is a funny gift at dinner."

Rosalie took a big bite of noodles. She drank her water. The duck watched.

"You can't eat," Rosalie told the duck. "You're a toy, not an animal." She fed the duck a pretend bite anyway.

The duck got a tiny carrot kiss on its beak. "Quack," said Rosalie. Mom smiled and gave Rosalie one more spoonful of peas.

Rosalie held the duck up high. "Dinner for everyone!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Jaxon went to Mia's house. Mia had a drum. It went boom, boom, boom.

"Listen," said Mia's mom. She sang a song. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She clapped her hands on every boom. Jaxon watched her hands. Up, down. Up, down.

Could he do that too? Jaxon clapped. His claps were too fast. The song ran ahead of him. He tried again. He waited for the boom. Then he clapped. Boom, clap! Boom, clap! Now his hands matched the drum.

Mia's baby brother was so young. He could not talk yet. But he heard the claps. He clapped his little hands too. He did not stop when the song did. His claps went on and on. Then he laughed so big he fell over.

Mia sang the star song. Jaxon knew the words now. He sang "like a diamond in the sky." Mia's mom pointed at the window. The sun shone through a rainbow sticker. "A diamond!" said Jaxon. He clapped one more boom. The baby clapped back.
